transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-05-11
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 55 minutes
Attendees: Samar Patel (Redwood AE), Evan Liu (Redwood SE), Maya Ortiz (Redwood PM), Priya Shah (LynxOps VP Platform), Carlos Mendes (SRE Lead), Aisha Khan (FinOps), Tom Becker (DevOps)

Summary (auto): Quick console tour focusing on per-route cost attribution, anomaly detection, and Optimize recommendations. Customers interested in a short pilot and security details.

[00:00] Samar Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — we got about an hour, we'll aim for 50 minutes plus Q&A. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Priya Shah: Hi Priya here.
[00:10] Carlos Mendes: Carlos, yep.
[00:11] Aisha Khan: Aisha.
[00:12] Tom Becker: Tom.
[00:14] Evan Liu: Evan from Redwood.
[00:15] Maya Ortiz: Maya here.
[00:17] Samar Patel: Cool. So high level, today we'll show the Console per-route usage lenses, how billing breaks down to tokens and routes, the anomaly alerting that caught unexpected spend, and then a bit of Optimize — batching and quantization recommendations. We'll also touch on hosting modes and security. Any must-have items before we dive in?
[00:30] Priya Shah: The big one for us is showing finance-level visibility: Aisha wants to know exactly which product routes are driving spend, and whether the anomalies are from spikes or model changes. Also we need to know what data leaves our VPC if we go hosted.
[00:43] Aisha Khan: Yep, and also the contract terms for a pilot — we have a procurement window end of month so timeline matters.
[00:50] Samar Patel: Understood. We'll take notes and we have an action item for pilot pricing. Evan, want to start the demo?
[00:55] Evan Liu: Yup. Pulling up the Console — bear with me, screen share error — there we go. So first thing is the Usage Overview. You can see total tokens, request count, and dollars by day. This top-level view is what most teams start with.
[01:18] [02:35] Evan Liu: Now drilling into Routes — we call these "routes" but customers sometimes call them endpoints, or features. Each route has its own dashboard: throughput, p50/p95 latency, token distribution, and cost per thousand tokens. Over here you can group by model variant, which is helpful if you have a canary model alongside a stable model. Note: sometimes transcripts show model name as "Aurora-7b" but it's really our open model catalog mapping.
[02:48] Carlos Mendes: How granular is the cost attribution? Can we map down to a specific internal team or service?
[02:55] Evan Liu: Yes — cost attributes support route -> project tag -> team. You can push tags via the API or via SDK metadata. We also ingest route-level labels from your proxy if you want automated tagging.
[03:15] [04:30] Aisha Khan: When you say cost per thousand tokens, is that including infra overhead or just token compute? We need to reconcile with our internal billing.
[03:45] Evan Liu: Good question. In the Console cost view we show unit cost (compute + amortized infra and licensing) and you can toggle to show breakdown: GPU compute, pre/post-processing, and networking. For Dedicated it will show committed capacity amortization vs burst.
[04:02] Priya Shah: If we go dedicated, how does autoscaling affect cost reporting? We want predictable month-to-month billing.
[04:12] Evan Liu: Dedication uses reserved pools. Our accounting shows committed capacity credits applied first, then burst usage as separate line items. The Console will project monthly spend based on current usage and autoscaling policies.
[04:31] [07:10] Samar Patel: Let's click into an example anomaly we saw. Back in March we had a 3x spike on route "agent-qa" — Console flagged this as an anomaly. Evan, walk us through the detection and root-cause tool.
[05:00] Evan Liu: Sure. The anomaly engine looks at historical token rates per route, model variant, and input length skew. It fires alerts on deviations and surfaces top correlates: model change, rollout, or prefix shift. For this spike we correlated it to a newer prompt template that increased token length. The Console's diff view shows the before/after token distribution which made root cause obvious.
[05:36] Carlos Mendes: Is the anomaly detector configurable? We want quieter alerts during on-call.
[05:42] Evan Liu: Yep — thresholds, alert windows, and noise filtering by traffic buckets are configurable. You can route alerts to PagerDuty, Slack, or email.
[06:00] [09:00] Maya Ortiz: One thing to highlight — Optimize will propose batching or a different model quantization profile when it detects that latency vs cost tradeoff can be improved. It actually simulates token-level impact across historical traffic to show predicted savings.
[06:20] Aisha Khan: Do you have an example number? We care about unit economics.
[06:28] Evan Liu: On average we see customers save 18-32% on per-token cost from batching + KV cache across chat-like workloads. For some high-throughput routes batching alone can cut CPU/GPU time by over 40%, but latency-sensitive routes are left alone.
[06:48] [12:15] Tom Becker: Quick nit — you mentioned KV cache. For our use case with many short-turn interactions, how much does cache help vs batching?
[07:02] Evan Liu: KV cache helps when you have repeated context like long conversations or shared system prompts; batching helps when many concurrent short requests arrive. In your traffic sample, looks like a mix — Optimize will recommend a profile that uses light prefix caching plus small batching windows to keep latency under 200 ms for p95.
[07:35] [15:00] Priya Shah: Security questions: does the hosted flow store customer prompts? What about KMS/HSM integrations and audit logs?
[08:00] Samar Patel: Good question. For hosted we retain transient logs for debugging by default but you can opt-in/opt-out. For Private and Dedicated we can provide customer-managed KMS and ship audit logs to your SIEM. We have SOC 2 Type II evidence and can share a security pack.
[08:32] Aisha Khan: Are there data residency options? We have EU-only data requirements for some routes.
[08:40] Evan Liu: Yes — region pinning lets you serve specific routes from EU regions. For full air-gapped, our Private on-prem package is an option.
[09:00] [18:30] Carlos Mendes: On networking — if we choose VPC private deployment, how is egress handled? We need to keep traffic inside our firewall.
[09:30] Evan Liu: In VPC mode all inference compute sits inside your VPC and egress is controlled by your network config. Our control plane can still orchestrate, or you can self-host the control plane. We have docs on the handshake and cert rotation.
[09:52] [22:00] Samar Patel: Let's walk a quick live example. Evan, open route "payments-ner" — show token breakdown and cost waterfall.
[10:00] Evan Liu: Opening it now. So the waterfall shows tokens broken into prompt tokens, generation tokens, and post-processing. Below that is cost by model and by time of day. You can see that a small number of long inputs in late hours drove disproportionate cost on May 2nd.
[10:25] Priya Shah: That late-hour bump — can we create a guardrail to throttle or use a cheaper model variant?
[10:29] Evan Liu: Yep — routing policies let you set time-based fallbacks: if p95 latency or spend exceeds X, route to a cheaper model variant or to a cached response. You can also set rate limits per API key or route.
[11:05] [26:40] Tom Becker: I'm worried about token accounting accuracy. We run transformers locally too; how do we reconcile tokenization differences between our token counts and yours?
[11:30] Evan Liu: We publish tokenization rules and tokenizer versions used for each model in the Console. There's a token mapping export so you can reconcile counts. We also allow you to upload a mapping if you use a custom tokenizer.
[11:58] [30:00] Aisha Khan: Pricing for pilot — can we get a committed capacity credit and run a 2-week pilot for three routes? What happens after pilot if traffic spikes?
[12:10] Samar Patel: Yes, pilot agreements are flexible. We typically give a time-limited committed credit plus bandwidth for burst. After pilot, you can convert to Dedicated or continue hosted with negotiated SLOs. We'll include guardrails for burst billing during the pilot.
[12:35] Carlos Mendes: Any minimums on model size or hardware? We need to know if we can test with our large LLMs.
[12:45] Evan Liu: You can run anything within the catalog; for very large models we recommend Dedicated to control latency and cost. The Console will flag model-size estimates for each route so you can plan capacity.
[13:20] [34:10] Maya Ortiz: Quick UX note — you asked about per-team attribution. You can map routes to cost centers and then create scheduled reports sent to finance weekly. We also have CSV/BigQuery exports if you want to integrate into existing finops pipelines.
[13:40] Aisha Khan: BigQuery export is great. That makes reconciling with our billing easier.
[13:45] [38:00] Priya Shah: Ok can we talk timeline? Procurement window is tight. We'd need pilot to start next week ideally.
[14:05] Samar Patel: We can do that. Action items: Samar will send security packet and pilot pricing; Priya will share route list and sample traffic; Evan will schedule benchmarking.
[14:22] [41:00] Carlos Mendes: A technical question — if we pin a route to EU region but the control plane is global, any latency or metadata leakage concerns?
[14:35] Evan Liu: Control plane metadata is minimal (status, metrics) and can be configured to exclude payloads. We can also run a private control plane in your VPC for extra isolation.
[15:00] [44:00] Tom Becker: On alerts, can we tune anomaly detector to ignore expected spikes from nightly jobs?
[15:10] Evan Liu: Yes, you can create suppression windows and tag traffic as "batch" to exclude from realtime anomaly detection.
[15:30] [47:00] Aisha Khan: For pilot pricing I need a clear breakdown: committed credits, expected overage, and SLA credits.
[15:42] Samar Patel: We'll include a one-page pilot pricing PDF that shows committed credits, per-token overage, and how SLA uptime credits work.
[16:00] [50:00] Priya Shah: Sounds good. Two final asks: send SOC2 and KMS docs, and a short runbook for the benchmarking test.
[16:15] Samar Patel: Yes. We'll send both. Evan, any parting demo notes?
[16:25] Evan Liu: Just one: watch the Optimize recommendations tab — it's often the first place where teams see immediate wins. We'll also show a sample quantization plan in the benchmark.
[16:40] [54:00] Samar Patel: Great. Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the security packet and pilot docs. Expect an invite for the benchmark timeslots from Evan.
[16:50] Priya Shah: Thanks, talk soon.
[16:52] Meeting end.
